newsitem.title: USA: Apparent Calif. mass suicide victims wore shrouds.
newsitem.headline: Apparent Calif. mass suicide victims wore shrouds.

text.p: The bodies of 39 men and women, cloaked in purple shrouds, were found in a million-dollar California mansion in what police on Thursday said appeared to be a mass suicide.

Cmdr. Alan Fulmer of the San Diego County Sheriff's Department told an early-morning news conference the cause of death remained a mystery, but he ruled out gas poisoning. "There were no gas fumes in the house. The only smell coming out of that house was that of dead bodies," he said.

Fulmer said he believed the 39, including an undetermined number of women, took their lives in a ritual that left them appearing as though they had died peacefully in their sleep. "My supposition at this point is that it was a mass suicide."

He said all the victims were cloaked in purple, triangular shrouds covering their faces and chests and wore black trousers and black tennis shoes. He refused to speculate on whether they belonged to a religious cult, but broadcast reports said the dead belonged to a religious group that designed computer web pages.

Fulmer said a previous description of the victims as all males between the ages of 18 and 24 was incorrect. "There were some women among the victims and some of the victims were over the age of 24," he said, explaining that sheriff's deputies did not examine the bodies on first entering the house.

He said the victims were found lying on mattresses or cots with their hands at their sides as if they had fallen asleep. No suicide notes were found and there were no signs of physical trauma, adding to the mystery around their deaths.
Deputies were alerted to a problem at the $1.6 million mansion in the exclusive San Diego suburb of Rancho Santa Fe on Wednesday by an anonymous caller who asked police to check on the residents.

Some 30 detectives and crime laboratory technicians from the San Diego Sheriff's Department were working on the case, Fulmer said, and experts from the Los Angeles Coroner's Office would be joining them later. The bodies were left in the house overnight and were expected to be removed during the day.

Milton Silverman, a lawyer for the owner of the house, was quoted by local TV stations as saying it had been rented to a religious computer group led by a man called "Father John" and that its members, who did not drink alcohol or smoke and were celibate, were sent to Americans as "angels."

Tom Goodspeed, general manager of the San Diego Polo Club, said members of the group solicited the club's business and he hired them to create a web site. "They were very genuine people, very talented in their skills with computers," he told Reuters. Most had "buzz cuts" and wore dark clothing, he said.
"Even though their appearance was a little strange, they were more than capable of creating our web page."
Beverly Hills businessman Nick Matzorkis said an employee who is a former member of the group received a packet from the group on Wednesday saying its members had committed suicide.

Matzorkis, who said it was he who called police and asked them to check the house, told CNN the package also contained a video showing the members saying goodbye and that they appeared happy about their decision.

Broadcast reports said the house had been for sale for at least a year but real estate agents had a hard time making appointments to show it to prospective buyers because its occupants were often conducting religious ceremonies.
Silverman said the occupants told the owner they did not want anyone to visit the house this week. "He said they asked that the house not be shown this week because it was their Holy Week."
Real estate agent Scott Warren, who had showed the house recently, described to ABC's "Nightline" a "bizarre" scene in which the occupants considered the residence a "temple."
Broadcast reports said the house was filled with computers and there were bunk beds in the bedrooms in a dormitory-style sleeping arrangement.

News of the apparent suicides quickly spread through the affluent neighbourhood, shocking residents. One neighbour, Bill Strong, told reporters the mansion was owned by a man named Sam Koutchesahani who had rented it to people "from out of state" in October.

He said those who lived in the house were "middle-aged, men and women." The mansion is surrounded by a brick wall in a community of palatial estates known as the "Beverly Hills of San Diego" some 20 miles (32 km) north of San Diego.

Police said there was no sign the deaths were related to Saturday's incident in Quebec when five members of a doomsday cult called the Solar Temple died in a blazing house in an apparent ritual suicide pact. In 1994 and 1995, 69 members of the Solar Temple cult died in fires in Canada and Switzerland.
